newsitem.title: USA: GAO says Congress should not fund some IRS requests.
newsitem.headline: GAO says Congress should not fund some IRS requests.

text.p: Congress should not give the Internal Revenue Service some of the money it requested for 1998 until the tax agency takes care of problems, the General Accounting Office said Tuesday.
The non-partisan watchdog agency also recommended that Congress rescind $36 million appropriated to the IRS for the current year because of cancelled projects.

The IRS budget request for fiscal 1998, which starts Oct. 1, includes $131 million for developmental information systems. The administration has proposed a $1 billion capital account for information technology investments at the IRS over two years, the GAO said.

"Congress should consider not funding either the $131 million request or the capital account until management and technical weaknesses in IRS' modernization program are resolved," Lynda Willis, GAO tax policy director, said in a statement for a House Ways and Means subcommittee hearing.

The budget request says the IRS does not know how it plans to spend the $131 million because the plan has not been completed, and the administration's $1 billion two-year proposal was not based on analytical data or derived using formal cost-estimating techniques, Willis said.

On the other hand, an $84 million request for 1998 may be insufficient to deal with the so-called "millenium bug," Willis said. Computers worldwide, which often read only the last two digits of the year, must be converted before the turn of the century so they will not read 2000 as 1900.
The agency's basic budget request for fiscal 1998 is for $7.4 billion, compared with the $7.2 billion appropriated for 1997, she said.
The Treasury Department unveiled Monday a five-point program to modernize the IRS, including stronger Treasury oversight of the agency.
House Ways and Means Committee Chairman Bill Archer told the hearing that Treasury's five points were "all sensible" but the plan did not go far enough.
"It really is a fig leaf on the problem," the Texas Republican said. "The plan's main shortcoming is it doesn't go far enough."
Increased Treasury oversight of the IRS would only address part of the problem, while "the crux of the problem is the tax system itself," said Archer, an advocate of simplifying the tax code.
